messages.author: 681b1f85f070a606
messages.subject: Stat_smooth
parts:
Hi,

I created a stat_smooth graph. Is there a way to see actual points?
For example I want the value of points (0,Y) and some point else
(X,Y).

Thanks,
Oshrat.

messages.author: 5f8b51633aa2f2a1
messages.subject: Re: Stat_smooth
parts:
But of course!

Say you're working with the mpg data set, you could do something like:

p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = cty, y = hwy)) + stat_smooth()

print(p) # To just get the smoother

print(p + geom_point()) # To add the points on top

Alternatively, with qplot()

qplot(cty, hwy, data = mpg) + stat_smooth()

should show both. [Note that for this data set, you might want to
jitter the points a little before use or using geom_jitter() instead
of geom_point()]

Short answer: yes, just stick +geom_point() on the end of whatever
plotting code you have now.

Hope this helps,

Michael

messages.subject: Re: Stat_smooth
parts:
Hi,

Thanks for the answer, but that wasn't my intention.
What I meant is not changing the graph appearance, but a way to know
point's actual value.
In the graph you can see a line and a smoother. What I'm looking for
is a way to know certain points value on the line, say at x=0, what is
the y value, and the largest value of x, again, what is the y value.
this is what I did:
c <- ggplot(survey, aes(Time, Willingness))
> c + stat_smooth(method="loess")

Thanks,
Oshrat

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Stat_smooth
parts:
Hi:

One way to see what has been plotted is to call the ggplot_build()
function in 0.9.x. For Michael's example, try
p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = cty, y = hwy)) + stat_smooth()

ggplot_build(p)

and look at the list element $data[[1]]. I can't guarantee that in
your problem you'll be able to find the corresponding fitted value of
the loess curve at x = 0, in part because the range of your data was
not revealed, but you should be able to extract the prediction at the
maximum x value. By default, geom_smooth() splits the x-range from the
observed data into 80 equally spaced points and returns the predicted
values from loess() at those points (using the default arguments
unless otherwise specified). The information in $data[[1]] is used to
render the smoother with 95% pointwise confidence intervals using the
estimated standard error at each x using a t-based confidence
procedure.

Another approach is to do the loess() fit outside of ggplot2, define a
set of values at which you want predictions and send the corresponding
output into a separate data frame that you can import into the
ggplot() call as separate layers. That would give you more control
over what is plotted, but also requires a little more work on your
part.

HTH,
Dennis
